No. 8· 17 September 2026· Global, Italy in focus· Illustrated edition
In three lines

The world

PYMNTS, Variety · 10 Sep 2026

OpenAI locks its own advertising competitors out of ChatGPT

OpenAI stopped selling ChatGPT ad placements to companies competing with its own image and audio generation tools. Adobe found out without advance warning: it lost the ability to promote its Firefly image generator inside ChatGPT. The restriction landed the same week OpenAI shipped ChatGPT Images 2.5 and its new voice product, ChatGPT Live, in the exact categories it had just closed to outside advertisers. Adobe's Doug Wyatt: "ChatGPT is narrowing both the paid and organic discovery pathways for tools in categories it now competes in directly." OpenAI has disclosed ad revenue targets of $2.5 billion this year, rising to $11 billion in 2027, $25 billion in 2028, $53 billion in 2029 and $100 billion by 2030.

Why it mattersOpenAI is trying to be the marketplace and a seller inside it at the same time. That is a specific, well-litigated kind of conflict of interest, and it is exactly the shape of the historical bridge below.
AdExchanger, Digiday · 2 Sep 2026

Google's ad tech remedies stay sealed, deadline lands the day before this issue

Judge Leonie Brinkema rejected every structural remedy the Department of Justice asked for, including forcing Google to divest AdX or DoubleClick, and instead accepted a modified version of the behavioral remedies both sides proposed: interoperability requirements and rules meant to stop Google depressing publisher ad rates. The memorandum spelling out exactly what those rules require stays under seal. Parties had 14 days from the 2 September ruling to request redactions, putting the deadline at 16 September, one day before this issue. PubMatic called it a step toward "a level playing field." CartographAI's Jay Friedman was more skeptical, telling AdExchanger it is still unclear whether rival ad servers get real access to Google's buy-side demand "as opposed to access on paper." Google's VP for regulatory affairs, Lee-Anne Mulholland, said the company was "very pleased the Court rejected the DOJ's proposal to break apart tools that help small businesses."

Why it mattersA win framed as "no breakup" can still change the daily mechanics of ad buying, but nobody outside the courtroom will know which until the seal comes off.
IAB · 10 Sep 2026

IAB raises its 2026 US ad spend growth forecast to 12.3%

The Interactive Advertising Bureau revised its 2026 US advertising growth forecast up to 12.3%, 2.8 points above the 9.5% it projected in January. Social media was raised to 16.5% growth, connected TV to 15.6%, commerce media to 13.6%.

Why it mattersThe upgrade midway through the year signals real budget is still moving into the fastest-growing formats, not just forecasts catching up to hope.
Adweek · 15 to 17 Sep 2026

Brandweek 2026 opens in Atlanta with Adweek's first dedicated AI day

Brandweek returned to Atlanta this week with Coca-Cola global CMO Manuel Arroyo, Starbucks global chief brand officer Tressie Lieberman and FIGS CMO Bene Eaton among the speakers. New for 2026: a full AI Accelerator Day dedicated to how brands use AI for personalization, efficiency and new marketing, positioned as tactical training rather than a keynote showcase.

Why it mattersWhen a legacy marketing conference builds an entire day around AI fluency instead of folding it into a panel, that is the industry admitting the skill gap is now operational, not conceptual.
Marketing Week · Sep 2026

Pandora's new CMO says the brand got "too polished"

Jennie Farmer, promoted to CMO in January after Pandora's former marketing chief Berta de Pablos-Barbier moved into the CEO seat, told Marketing Week the brand has "been a little bit too polished" in social, pushing "beautiful brand campaigns" into channels that reward something rougher. Her fix leans on a wider, more demographically mixed set of ambassadors, from Pamela Anderson to Tyla, and a pivot toward creators, fashion moments and experiential work over Pandora's historically TV-heavy media mix.

Why it mattersThis is a jewellery brand's CMO diagnosing the exact same problem this brief keeps tracking in the content section, polish reads as content, roughness reads as evidence.

Social trends

Newengen · Sep 2026

"I'm With Max"

  • Confessional lip-sync format: creators name whatever person, task or obligation is quietly running their entire calendar this month, "Max" standing in as a placeholder name for the thing that owns you.
  • Newengen flags it as a fresh format still climbing, not yet saturated.
  • Status: fresh, climbing.
Newengen · Sep 2026

"Someone's Gotta Hold It Down"

  • Hometown-pride format: creators flip the usual small-town-escape narrative into deadpan pride, framing staying put as the harder, more admirable choice.
  • Early-stage per Newengen's September tracking.
  • Status: early, worth watching alongside the week's wave of flag-waving brand campaigns (Jeep, below).
Newengen · Sep 2026

"Flop-Core"

  • Anti-highlight-reel format: creators post the failed take, the burnt dinner, the missed audition, instead of the polished win, sometimes captioning it as the actual content rather than an outtake.
  • Early-stage per Newengen.
  • Status: early, but lines up precisely with Pandora's CMO admitting its own feed had gotten "too polished."
Why it mattersThe platform's own trend trackers note a lifecycle split worth planning around: audio-led trends peak in 7 to 10 days while format-led trends like these three run 3 to 4 weeks before saturating. None of this week's three trends needs a viral sound to work, which is exactly why they will likely outlast this week's news cycle.

Campaigns & brand moves

Stellantis, Autoblog · 9 Sep 2026

Jeep turns its 85th birthday into a national identity claim

Jeep launched "This Is Jeep Country," a fully integrated campaign across TV, streaming, digital, social and experiential media, timed to the brand's 85th anniversary and the opening of NFL season. The campaign runs across NFL programming and CTV platforms including Disney+, Paramount+, Max and Peacock, featuring the brand's full vehicle range, Wrangler through the new Recon, moving through American landscapes with no product-spec talk, just landscape and flag.

Why it mattersJeep is betting that in a year when patriotism-as-marketing is contested territory, leaning all the way in, rather than softening the message, is the safer read on where NFL-watching America's mood actually sits this September.
MediaBrief, TechTimes · 8 Sep 2026

Samsung lands its global foldables blitz one day before Apple's keynote

Samsung's "Welcome to Foldables" campaign took over Times Square, Piccadilly Circus, Shibuya Station and two landmark screens in Seoul on 8 September, one day ahead of Apple's annual product event, marking eight generations of Galaxy Z engineering under three claims: "Ultra Thin," "The World's Lightest Fold," "Built to Outlast." The Galaxy Z8 series is available across 106 global markets.

Why it mattersThis is not a product launch, it is a pure timing play, buying the world's most expensive landmark screens for the one day when the entire industry's attention is guaranteed to be pointed at a rival's stage.
Media Key, Global Storytelling · 10 Sep 2026

Warner Bros Italia turns a fictional cocktail into a real product

For the Italian release of "Amori & Incantesimi 2" ("Practical Magic 2"), Warner Bros Entertainment Italia partnered with Classy Cocktails to turn the "Midnight Margarita," the drink Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman's characters mix in their kitchen in the original film, into an actual ready-to-drink product. It is the first Italian partnership between a ready-to-drink cocktail brand and a Warner Bros film, sold as a limited-edition box exclusively on Classy Cocktails' e-commerce site through September, paired with a second cocktail tied to Volcan de Mi Tierra tequila.

Why it mattersThe mechanism is not "movie tie-in merchandise," it is converting a prop that already lives rent-free in fans' heads into something they can actually buy and drink during the exact week the sequel is in theatres.

What is working in content

Newengen · Sep 2026

Trend lifecycle data gives creators a planning window

Newengen's own September trend tracking states audio-driven trends peak within 7 to 10 days of emerging, while format-driven trends, no specific sound required, run 3 to 4 weeks before saturating. This is a single agency's aggregated observation, not an audited platform statistic, and is flagged as such.

Why it mattersIt is a concrete argument for which trend type is worth a brand's production time. A sound-based trend is a same-week-or-never bet; a format like "Flop-Core" or "Someone's Gotta Hold It Down" gives a brand a month to actually plan something instead of scrambling to lip-sync in time.
Instagram / TikTok trend data · Sep 2026

Specificity keeps beating vague uplift

Two of this week's fresh formats both work by replacing a vague claim with a concrete, checkable detail: "I'm With Max" names an actual thing instead of saying "I've been busy," and "Flop-Core" shows the actual failed take instead of describing "growth through failure." Pandora's own CMO independently arrived at the same diagnosis about the brand's paid content this week.

Why it mattersThree unrelated sources, two platform trend formats and one CMO interview, converged on the same finding in the same seven-day window without citing each other. That kind of convergence is a stronger signal than any single data point in this brief.

The historical bridge

New Jersey, 1968

Carterfone: the network that could pick its own competitors

Thomas Carter, a Texas inventor, built a device that let two-way radio users patch into the phone network. AT&T's tariff banned all "foreign attachments," equipment not made or approved by AT&T, from touching its network, and the company could legally disconnect any customer who used one. AT&T framed the ban as protecting network integrity. It also happened to protect Western Electric, AT&T's own equipment manufacturing arm, from every competitor. The FCC had already cracked the door open in 1956 with Hush-A-Phone, a plastic privacy cup for handsets AT&T had also tried to ban. In the Carterfone case, the FCC ruled the blanket foreign-attachment ban unlawful and ordered AT&T to open its tariffs to outside equipment, a decision now recognized as the first domino toward the breakup of the Bell System in 1984.

Why it still holds. OpenAI restricting ChatGPT ad access for Adobe's Firefly, the same week it ships its own competing image and voice tools, is the Carterfone problem with a chat window instead of a phone jack. AT&T got to decide what could connect to its network while also selling the equipment that connected to it; OpenAI gets to decide who can advertise on its platform while also shipping the products those advertisers compete with. The FCC needed twelve years, 1956 to 1968, to force that conflict open. Nobody has built the equivalent regulator for AI platforms yet.
